analysis.one_liner: Gives workers at medium and large employers ten weeks of unpaid maternity or adoption leave with job protection.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a House vote; it sat in subcommittees from November 1989 until that Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have let eligible employees take ten workweeks of unpaid leave for the birth or adoption of a child, with the right to return to their same or an equivalent job. Employers with 50 or more employees would have had to keep health coverage in force during the leave, and the Labor Department could fine violators up to $10,000. Workers would first have to use up any accrued paid leave, and the unpaid weeks would count against later leave. The bill was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to two subcommittees, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees at employers with 50 or more workers who have worked at least 12 months and 1,250 hours in the prior year — mainly new mothers and adoptive parents — who would get ten weeks of protected leave, continued health coverage, and the right to their job back, with federal enforcement behind those rights.

how_it_helps.text: Eligible employees would be entitled to ten workweeks of unpaid leave in any 24-month period for the birth of a child or the placement of a child for adoption, taken in consecutive weeks.
On return, employees would be restored to their former position or an equivalent one with equivalent pay and benefits, and would keep benefits earned before the leave.
Employers would have to continue group health plan coverage during the leave at the same level as if the employee had kept working.

The Labor Secretary could assess civil penalties of up to $10,000, seek court orders, and employees could sue for reinstatement and lost wages and benefits, with attorney's fees available to the prevailing party.
The bill would not weaken stronger maternity leave already guaranteed by a union contract, benefit plan, or state or local law.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — those with 50 or more eligible employees — would bear the cost of holding jobs open, continuing health coverage during leaves, and compliance and potential penalties; workers themselves would finance the leave by going without pay after exhausting accrued paid leave.

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid, and workers must exhaust all accrued sick and vacation leave before using it, so the benefit mainly helps those who can afford weeks without income.
Smaller employers (under 50 eligible employees) and workers with less than 12 months or 1,250 hours of service are excluded entirely.

Employers may deny restoration to the highest-paid 10 percent of employees (or the five highest-paid, whichever is greater) to prevent substantial economic injury, and may deny restoration to anyone who misses the written notice deadlines.
Employees lose no accrued benefits, but they do not accrue seniority or new benefits during the leave, and a failure to return to work shortens their later continuation health coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the bill offered real, enforceable protections — a guaranteed job back and continued health coverage during leave — at a modest, targeted cost to mid-sized and large employers. Its main weakness is that the leave is unpaid and narrower than the state laws and later federal standard, leaving out small businesses, newer workers, and anyone who cannot absorb weeks without a paycheck. It was a deliberately modest floor, not a paid-leave guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in October 1989, referred to the Education and Labor Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, and never came back out; the two-year Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Timothy J. Penny introduced the Maternity Leave Act of 1989 in the House on October 11, 1989, joined by three cosponsors (two Democrats and one Republican).
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor the day it was introduced.
On November 13, 1989, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards and the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations.
No further action was taken before the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, so the bill never reached the House floor or the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Covered employers were better off: they never had to grant the ten weeks of protected leave, continue health coverage during it, or face the bill's penalties, because the bill died in subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; sponsorship was mostly Democratic but included one Republican, and the record shows no organized opposition.

industries.note: The bill would have required these employers to grant protected leave, keep health coverage in force during it, and hold jobs open, with civil penalties up to $10,000 for violations. Because the bill died, these costs never materialized.

Requiring employers to continue group health coverage during leave would keep premiums flowing during absences while ensuring new parents did not lose coverage. The effect on insurers is minor and runs alongside the public's interest in continuous coverage.
